groups.title: Resource hierarchy
groups.mechanism: Organization, folders, projects and resources define management and policy scope. Billing association and permission inheritance are related but distinct mechanisms.
groups.tradeOff: Shared structure simplifies governance while broad inherited permissions enlarge exposure.
groups.verify: Inspect effective access on one resource through every ancestor and role binding.

questions.question: What is a Google Cloud project?
questions.answer: A management boundary grouping resources, API enablement, quotas and billing association under an identifier and policy hierarchy.

questions.question: When should workloads use separate projects?
questions.answer: When ownership, environments, billing, quota or security boundaries benefit from separation and the operational overhead is justified.

questions.question: How does hierarchy affect access management?
questions.answer: Applicable inherited policies and resource-level rules contribute to effective access; inspect the actual evaluation rather than only one local binding.

questions.question: Why is a project name not a security boundary by itself?
questions.answer: Names express intent, while IAM, network policy and service configuration enforce access and isolation.

questions.question: How would you structure production and development resources?
questions.answer: Separate trust and operational boundaries, define least-privilege access and make shared infrastructure dependencies explicit and auditable.

groups.title: IAM and least privilege
groups.mechanism: IAM binds principals to roles at specific scopes, with additional policy controls affecting effective access. Authorization should follow workload needs rather than broad convenience.
groups.tradeOff: Granular roles improve isolation but require lifecycle and access-review ownership.
groups.verify: Test permitted and denied actions with the actual deployed principal.

questions.question: What is the difference between a principal and a role?
questions.answer: A principal is an identity; a role groups permissions that can be granted to a principal at an applicable resource scope.

questions.question: When should a predefined role be preferred to Owner?
questions.answer: When its permissions cover the required tasks with less privilege; avoid broad administrative access for ordinary workloads.

questions.question: How do service permissions differ from network reachability?
questions.answer: A request can reach an endpoint and still lack authorization, or have permission while network policy prevents connectivity.

questions.question: Why can inherited access surprise a resource owner?
questions.answer: An ancestor binding may grant permissions even when the resource's own policy appears restrictive.

questions.question: How would you investigate an unexpected permission denial?
questions.answer: Identify the effective principal, requested permission, resource scope and applicable policies; use audit evidence rather than repeatedly widening roles.

groups.title: Workload identities
groups.mechanism: Workloads should obtain credentials through supported attached or federated identities rather than embedded long-lived keys.
groups.tradeOff: Short-lived credentials reduce persistent secret exposure while requiring correct trust configuration.
groups.verify: Run from the target platform and verify identity, audience and credential refresh failure behavior.

questions.question: What is a service account?
questions.answer: A workload identity that can receive permissions and authenticate under supported Google Cloud mechanisms.

questions.question: When is Workload Identity Federation useful?
questions.answer: When external or platform workloads need trusted short-lived access without distributing long-lived service-account keys.

questions.question: How does service-account impersonation differ from sharing a key?
questions.answer: An authorized principal obtains scoped short-lived credentials through a controlled mechanism instead of copying a persistent private key.

questions.question: Why are downloaded service-account keys risky?
questions.answer: They can be copied, leaked and used outside the intended environment until revoked, with difficult ownership and rotation management.

questions.question: How would you migrate away from static cloud keys?
questions.answer: Identify each consumer, configure supported identity trust, grant minimal roles, test refresh and remove keys after verified transition.

groups.title: Regions and zones
groups.mechanism: Regions and zones define placement and failure domains, while each service has its own replication and availability model.
groups.tradeOff: Geographic redundancy improves resilience but adds cost, latency and consistency decisions.
groups.verify: Disable or isolate one failure domain in a controlled exercise and observe actual recovery.

questions.question: How do regions and zones differ?
questions.answer: A region is a geographic area containing zones; zones represent deployment and failure-isolation domains within that region.

questions.question: When is multi-zone deployment sufficient?
questions.answer: When the required availability model tolerates regional failure and the service's data plus compute distribution actually spans zones.

questions.question: Does choosing a regional resource prove every dependency is regional?
questions.answer: No. Databases, secrets, networking and external integrations can have different placement or availability characteristics.

questions.question: Why can a multi-region application still have one failure point?
questions.answer: Its write authority, identity dependency, deployment process or routing configuration may remain concentrated in one region.

questions.question: How would you choose cross-region replication?
questions.answer: Start with RPO, RTO, write consistency and latency requirements, then validate the selected service's replication and failover capabilities.

groups.title: VPC networking
groups.mechanism: VPC configuration controls network paths, address ranges and filtering. Private addressing and IAM solve different security problems.
groups.tradeOff: Connectivity simplicity must be balanced with segmentation and address planning.
groups.verify: Trace DNS, route, firewall and service authorization separately for a failed connection.

questions.question: What is a VPC used for?
questions.answer: Defining a virtual network environment for applicable resources, including addressing, routes and connectivity controls.

questions.question: When should private connectivity be preferred?
questions.answer: When limiting public exposure and controlling service paths meets the workload's access requirements and supported service integration.

questions.question: How do firewall rules differ from IAM policy?
questions.answer: Firewall rules control network traffic under their scope; IAM determines whether a principal may perform an authorized service action.

questions.question: Why can two privately addressed services fail to connect?
questions.answer: Routes, ranges, DNS, firewall rules, service configuration or identity permissions may still block the request.

questions.question: How would you debug a database connection failure?
questions.answer: Check resolved destination and path, network policy, TLS and credentials, then pool acquisition and server limits as separate stages.

groups.title: Load balancing and ingress
groups.mechanism: Load balancing combines frontend protocols, backend health and routing policy. Product choice determines scope and supported behavior.
groups.tradeOff: Central ingress improves control but creates configuration and certificate ownership obligations.
groups.verify: Test host/path routes, unhealthy backends, certificates and traffic withdrawal.

questions.question: What is a cloud load balancer responsible for?
questions.answer: Accepting supported client traffic and distributing it to configured healthy backends according to routing and balancing policies.

questions.question: When should global versus regional balancing be evaluated?
questions.answer: When traffic locality, service placement, failover needs and supported frontend/backend capabilities require different scopes.

questions.question: How does a health check affect backend selection?
questions.answer: Its configured result influences eligibility, but it may not represent every business dependency or request path.

questions.question: Why can a healthy backend still return application failures?
questions.answer: The health check can test a cheaper or different path than authenticated, database-backed user operations.

questions.question: How would you validate an ingress migration?
questions.answer: Replay hosts, paths, protocols and error cases, verify TLS plus headers and test backend drain behavior before shifting broad traffic.

groups.title: Compute Engine
groups.mechanism: Virtual machines provide control over guest runtime and machine resources. Instance groups and templates add managed replication and rollout behavior.
groups.tradeOff: VM control includes patching, image, capacity and lifecycle responsibilities.
groups.verify: Recreate an instance from its declared template and verify application plus data recovery.

questions.question: When is Compute Engine a suitable choice?
questions.answer: When workload requirements need VM-level runtime control, supported machine capabilities or operational patterns that managed application platforms do not fit.

questions.question: What is an instance template used for?
questions.answer: Describing repeatable VM configuration that can be used by managed instance groups and related provisioning workflows.

questions.question: How does an instance group improve availability?
questions.answer: It can maintain desired instance count and distribute or replace instances according to its configuration and failure-domain support.

questions.question: Why should application state not depend on one VM's ephemeral files?
questions.answer: Replacement or failure can lose local transient state. Store durable state in an appropriate persistent system with tested recovery.

questions.question: How would you roll out a VM-based service safely?
questions.answer: Use immutable tested images or templates, controlled replacement, health criteria and backward-compatible shared data plus a rehearsed rollback.

groups.title: Cloud Run
groups.mechanism: Cloud Run runs supported container workloads under a managed execution and scaling model. Instance concurrency, startup and service limits must fit dependencies.
groups.tradeOff: Managed scaling reduces infrastructure work but can multiply downstream demand quickly.
groups.verify: Test cold starts, concurrent requests, instance termination and database connection counts.

questions.question: When is Cloud Run a good fit?
questions.answer: For compatible containerized services or jobs where managed infrastructure and demand-based scaling fit runtime and operational requirements.

questions.question: What does per-instance concurrency control?
questions.answer: How many requests an instance may handle concurrently under the configured service model; it is not a database-capacity guarantee.

questions.question: How can scale-out overload a shared database?
questions.answer: Each new instance can create its own pool, multiplying potential connections and concurrent queries beyond database capacity.

questions.question: Why should background work outlive a request only through a supported design?
questions.answer: CPU allocation, instance lifecycle and shutdown behavior depend on configuration; untracked in-process work can be lost.

questions.question: How would you configure a database-backed Cloud Run service?
questions.answer: Budget total connections across possible instances, bound per-instance work, set deadlines and verify identity, network connectivity and termination behavior.

groups.title: GKE fundamentals
groups.mechanism: GKE manages Kubernetes infrastructure while application owners still define resource, probe, security and deployment behavior.
groups.tradeOff: Orchestration flexibility adds configuration and operational complexity.
groups.verify: Reschedule a pod, drain a node and verify routing plus state recovery.

questions.question: What does GKE provide?
questions.answer: A managed Kubernetes environment with supported control-plane and cluster capabilities; applications still need correct workload configuration.

questions.question: When should GKE be preferred to a simpler managed runtime?
questions.answer: When Kubernetes-specific scheduling, networking, ecosystem or workload control justifies the additional operational surface.

questions.question: How do requests and limits affect a pod?
questions.answer: They influence scheduling and runtime resource constraints under Kubernetes behavior; misconfiguration can cause throttling, eviction or failed placement.

questions.question: Why can a readiness probe cause a service-wide outage?
questions.answer: A shared dependency failure can mark every pod unready if the policy removes all usable capacity instead of supporting deliberate degradation.

questions.question: How would you verify a GKE rollout?
questions.answer: Exercise startup, health, scaling, node disruption and termination while checking user-visible latency, resource pressure and persisted work recovery.

groups.title: Cloud Storage
groups.mechanism: Object storage addresses immutable object generations rather than arbitrary shared filesystem mutation. Access, lifecycle and concurrency rules must be explicit.
groups.tradeOff: Durability and scale are useful but request, transfer and retention costs need ownership.
groups.verify: Race object updates using generation preconditions and test lifecycle plus authorization rules.

questions.question: What kind of storage is Cloud Storage?
questions.answer: Managed object storage organized into buckets and named objects, with service-specific consistency, access and lifecycle capabilities.

questions.question: When should a signed URL be used?
questions.answer: For controlled temporary access to a specific object operation, with constrained lifetime and permissions rather than broad bucket credentials.

questions.question: How do generation preconditions protect updates?
questions.answer: They can require an expected object generation or existence condition, preventing an operation from blindly overwriting a changed object.

questions.question: Why is object storage not a drop-in local filesystem?
questions.answer: Atomic rename, random in-place updates and directory assumptions differ; design using object operations and their explicit contracts.

questions.question: How would you design a safe upload workflow?
questions.answer: Limit size and type, authorize destination, verify completion and ownership, and recover or expire incomplete/unreferenced objects without deleting valid uploads.

groups.title: Cloud SQL
groups.mechanism: Cloud SQL manages supported relational database operations, but schema, queries, pooling and application transaction semantics remain application responsibilities.
groups.tradeOff: Managed operations reduce toil without eliminating capacity and recovery planning.
groups.verify: Test failover and maintenance effects on pooled connections plus retry-safe transactions.

questions.question: What does Cloud SQL manage?
questions.answer: A managed relational database service for supported engines, with operational capabilities such as backups and availability options depending on configuration.

questions.question: When should a connector or supported proxy integration be considered?
questions.answer: When its supported identity and connection-management capabilities fit the application, while separately understanding its networking prerequisites.

questions.question: How does high availability differ from a read replica?
questions.answer: HA targets availability of the primary service; a replica serves a distinct replication/read role with its own lag and promotion considerations.

questions.question: Why does a read replica not guarantee read-your-writes?
questions.answer: Replication can lag, so a recent primary commit may not yet be visible on the replica.

questions.question: How would you validate Cloud SQL failover readiness?
questions.answer: Exercise connection recovery, transaction ambiguity, application deadlines and authoritative data reconciliation rather than checking only that the instance returns healthy.

groups.title: Spanner
groups.mechanism: Spanner provides a distributed relational service with its own transaction, key-distribution and query model. Schema and key choices affect data placement and load.
groups.tradeOff: Strong transactional capabilities do not remove latency, hotspot or cost trade-offs.
groups.verify: Load realistic key distributions and retry supported transaction aborts safely.

questions.question: When is Spanner worth evaluating?
questions.answer: When relational consistency, scale and geographic requirements exceed simpler database options enough to justify its cost and application model.

questions.question: Why does primary-key design matter in a distributed database?
questions.answer: It influences distribution and access locality; concentrated writes can create hotspots despite large aggregate service capacity.

questions.question: How should transaction aborts be handled?
questions.answer: Through supported retry semantics that recompute the transaction from fresh state without repeating irreversible external side effects.

questions.question: Why can a low-volume test conceal a key hotspot?
questions.answer: Small datasets and uniform traffic may not reproduce a production concentration of writes or reads on one key range.

questions.question: How would you migrate to Spanner responsibly?
questions.answer: Validate schema and SQL compatibility, key distribution, transaction behavior and latency under representative load, with explicit data verification and cutover recovery.

groups.title: Firestore
groups.mechanism: Firestore's document and query model has explicit indexing, transaction and access-rule behavior. Document design follows access patterns and update contention.
groups.tradeOff: Denormalization can simplify reads while increasing coordinated-update and storage costs.
groups.verify: Test missing fields, index requirements, concurrent transactions and authorization boundaries.

questions.question: When is Firestore suitable?
questions.answer: When a managed document model and its supported queries, transactions and client integration fit the workload better than relational joins.

questions.question: How should document boundaries be chosen?
questions.answer: From read/update patterns, size limits, contention and ownership rather than mechanically mapping each relational row.

questions.question: Why can a query require a new index?
questions.answer: Firestore supports queries through its indexing model, and compound query shapes can require explicit index configuration.

questions.question: Why must transaction callbacks avoid external side effects?
questions.answer: Supported transaction retries can run application logic again, potentially repeating email, payment or external API effects.

questions.question: How would you maintain derived documents safely?
questions.answer: Use durable operation identity and controlled update/retry behavior, then reconcile partial changes instead of assuming all denormalized copies stay atomic automatically.

groups.title: BigQuery
groups.mechanism: BigQuery is an analytical system optimized for large-scale queries rather than ordinary per-request transactional updates. Partition and projection choices influence work and cost.
groups.tradeOff: Analytical flexibility can become expensive without bounded query patterns and ownership.
groups.verify: Inspect processed data, partition pruning and correctness on late-arriving records.

questions.question: When should BigQuery be used?
questions.answer: For analytical processing and reporting over large datasets, not as a casual replacement for an operational transaction database.

questions.question: Why select only needed columns?
questions.answer: Column projection can reduce scanned data and work, while improving clarity and limiting unnecessary data exposure.

questions.question: How does partition pruning help?
questions.answer: Suitable predicates can restrict which partitions are scanned, reducing work under the table's partitioning and query rules.

questions.question: Why can LIMIT fail to make a query cheap?
questions.answer: Limiting returned rows does not necessarily limit all scanned or processed input data.

questions.question: How would you build a reliable daily analytics report?
questions.answer: Define event-time boundaries, late data, deduplication and schema evolution, then validate totals and cost on representative partitions.

groups.title: Pub/Sub
groups.mechanism: Pub/Sub separates publication from subscription delivery. Acknowledgment timing and delivery guarantees must be interpreted within the configured feature scope.
groups.tradeOff: Asynchronous buffering improves decoupling but introduces backlog, redelivery and ordering decisions.
groups.verify: Lose an acknowledgment, delay processing and restart consumers while checking durable effects.

questions.question: What does a Pub/Sub subscription represent?
questions.answer: A delivery relationship through which consumers receive messages from a topic under the configured acknowledgment and retention behavior.

questions.question: When is an ordering key useful?
questions.answer: When related messages need supported ordered delivery within a defined scope; it does not establish universal ordering across independent keys.

questions.question: Does an acknowledgment make an external database write atomic?
questions.answer: No. Database commit and message progress are separate boundaries unless a supported explicit protocol coordinates them.

questions.question: Why can a message be delivered again after successful processing?
questions.answer: The effect can commit before acknowledgment succeeds, or the acknowledgment deadline and delivery state can permit redelivery.

questions.question: How would you use an exactly-once delivery feature carefully?
questions.answer: Read its subscription and regional scope, verify acknowledgment outcomes and retain idempotency for external side effects and application-level retries.

groups.title: Secrets and configuration
groups.mechanism: Secret Manager stores secret versions with access policy, while applications still own retrieval, caching, rotation and accidental-exposure prevention.
groups.tradeOff: Frequent retrieval improves freshness but adds dependency and latency considerations.
groups.verify: Rotate versions during traffic and test denied access plus unavailable retrieval.

questions.question: Why use Secret Manager instead of source-controlled credentials?
questions.answer: It provides controlled secret storage and versioned access without distributing credentials through code history or packaged artifacts.

questions.question: When should a workload fetch a secret?
questions.answer: According to a deliberate startup or refresh policy balancing availability, rotation latency and the integration's credential behavior.

questions.question: How do secret versions affect rotation?
questions.answer: Consumers need a defined version-selection and refresh strategy, including overlap and removal of older credentials when supported.

questions.question: Why can reading the latest secret once fail during rotation?
questions.answer: A long-lived client may keep the old credential indefinitely, or new credentials may not be active at the remote system yet.

questions.question: How would you prevent secret leakage in diagnostics?
questions.answer: Redact values, restrict management endpoints, avoid logging credential-bearing URLs or payloads and test both normal and exceptional paths.

groups.title: Monitoring and SLOs
groups.mechanism: Cloud telemetry must represent user outcomes and causal timing. Alerting should focus on actionable service degradation rather than every resource fluctuation.
groups.tradeOff: More signals aid diagnosis while high cardinality and noisy alerts increase cost and fatigue.
groups.verify: Inject a user-visible failure and verify metrics, trace linkage and actionable alert routing.

questions.question: What is an SLO?
questions.answer: A target for a defined service-level indicator over a period, such as successful requests within a latency threshold.

questions.question: When is error-budget burn useful?
questions.answer: When assessing how quickly current failures consume the allowed unreliability and whether intervention or rollout restraint is justified.

questions.question: How do logs, metrics and traces complement each other?
questions.answer: Logs provide events, metrics aggregate behavior and traces connect instrumented operations; correlation aligns them around a real request or business operation.

questions.question: Why is CPU-only alerting insufficient?
questions.answer: Users can experience timeouts from queues or dependencies while CPU is low, or high CPU can occur without breaching user targets.

questions.question: How would you control observability cost?
questions.answer: Bound labels, retention and sampling, prioritize actionable evidence and preserve necessary security plus failure visibility under explicit ownership.

groups.title: Deployment and supply chain
groups.mechanism: A deployable artifact needs provenance, controlled configuration and promotion criteria. Deployment tools do not guarantee schema or protocol compatibility.
groups.tradeOff: Automation speeds delivery while requiring trusted artifacts and explicit rollback conditions.
groups.verify: Promote the same artifact through environments and test mixed-version operation.

questions.question: Why promote an immutable artifact?
questions.answer: It reduces differences between tested and deployed code and makes provenance plus rollback identification clearer.

questions.question: When should deployment approval depend on business metrics?
questions.answer: When technical health can stay green while the release violates conversion, payment or data-processing invariants.

questions.question: How do service revisions help rollout control?
questions.answer: They identify deployed application configurations and can support controlled traffic changes under the selected platform's capabilities.

questions.question: Why can rebuilding for each environment weaken validation?
questions.answer: Each artifact may resolve different dependencies or inputs, so production can differ from what earlier tests exercised.

questions.question: How would you secure a cloud delivery pipeline?
questions.answer: Limit identity permissions, verify source/artifact provenance, isolate untrusted builds and require relevant compatibility plus behavioral checks before promotion.

groups.title: Scaling and cost
groups.mechanism: Scaling changes offered capacity and often increases demand on shared dependencies. Cost should be evaluated per useful outcome, including storage, transfer and idle resources.
groups.tradeOff: Reducing idle spend can increase cold-start latency or recovery requirements.
groups.verify: Load the workload, measure unit cost and inspect downstream saturation plus rejected requests.

questions.question: Why is autoscaling not a complete capacity plan?
questions.answer: Its signals, limits and reaction time may not match traffic bursts or the capacity of databases and external systems.

questions.question: When should minimum instances be considered?
questions.answer: When measured cold-start or readiness latency justifies keeping capacity warm under the chosen platform's behavior and cost model.

questions.question: How can egress influence architecture cost?
questions.answer: Data movement across regions, services or external boundaries can be material; verify current applicable billing rules rather than assuming transfer is free.

questions.question: Why can a budget alert fail to stop overspending?
questions.answer: An alert informs; it is not generally a hard universal service spending cap. Quotas and operational controls have different scopes.

questions.question: How would you optimize cloud cost responsibly?
questions.answer: Measure cost per successful operation, identify waste and bottlenecks, then compare rightsizing, retention and architecture changes against reliability requirements.

groups.title: Disaster recovery
groups.mechanism: Backups, replication and failover solve different recovery problems. Restoration must account for identity, routing, secrets and effects outside restored data.
groups.tradeOff: Tighter RPO/RTO requires additional capacity and practiced procedures.
groups.verify: Restore an isolated environment and verify critical business operations before claiming recovery.

questions.question: What should a cloud disaster-recovery plan include?
questions.answer: Objectives, dependencies, data restoration, traffic routing, identities, secrets, application artifacts and reconciliation ownership.

questions.question: When is multi-region deployment insufficient for disaster recovery?
questions.answer: When replicated corruption, missing backups or an untested control-plane dependency prevents restoring a correct usable state.

questions.question: How do backups protect against accidental deletion differently from replicas?
questions.answer: Backups preserve selected historical recovery points, while replicas can promptly reproduce the same unwanted deletion.

questions.question: Why must external effects be reconciled after restoration?
questions.answer: Payments or messages after the restored point may already exist outside the recovered database, creating duplicate or missing operational records.

questions.question: How would you prove the recovery plan works?
questions.answer: Execute it, measure RPO/RTO, verify integrity and authorized access, and reconcile event positions plus ambiguous business effects.
